sentences: The Fix: If the brain is burning less sugar, we give it another fuel.
Ketones are its backup fuel, and brains that take up less glucose (as in early Alzheimer's) still take up ketones normally (Cunnane, et al, 2016).
And one man's Alzheimer's improved markedly on coconut oil, and later on a ketone drink (Newport, et al, 2015).
In Parkinson's too, one small study with no comparison group showed large improvement on a ketogenic diet (VanItallie, et al, 2005).
In a bigger trial against a low-fat diet, the keto diet eased fatigue, sleepiness and thinking problems more, but movement improved about the same on both (Phillips, et al, 2018).
PQQ made mouse cells build more mitochondria, the parts of the cell that burn fuel (Chowanadisai, et al, 2010); whether it does that in the human brain hasn't been shown.

haiku: The paragraph is metronomic, with nearly every sentence following the same claim-plus-citation pattern at similar length, and its voice is impersonal and even-tempered, built as a tidy label, mechanism, then evidence sequence. That evenness reads machine-made, though an editor smoothing a human draft could produce the same effect.
sonnet: The paragraph is built as a steady march of study-per-sentence, each with the same claim, qualifier and citation pattern, and the sentences are similar in length and tone with little personal voice. It is orderly and even-handed in a way that reads assembled rather than spoken.
